\chapter{Four Verbs Two Languages Built Twice}
\label{ch:acabar-y-empezar}
\hlchaptermodality{382}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say empezar, acabar, pagar and quedar, and name four everyday actions.}

Complete ES-C382-quedar: name four everyday actions, and say which one you did today.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[empezar]{empezar — taking the first piece off}

\label{lesson:ES-C382-empezar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to jump}, then \emph{to dream}. (\emph{Saltar}; \emph{soñar}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el pan — something you begin by taking a piece off.
  \item el libro — something else you begin.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{em-pe-ZAR}, three beats with the weight on the last. The \emph{z} is the \emph{th} of \emph{think} in much of Spain and an \emph{s} across the Americas. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{empezar} — \textquotedblleft{}to begin.\textquotedblright{}

There is a noun hiding in the middle of it: \textbf{pieza}, a piece. The Academy's dictionary builds \emph{empezar} from \emph{en-} plus \emph{pieza}, and the picture that gives you is physical. To begin a thing is to take the first piece off it — the first slice of bread, the first page.

\emph{Pieza} itself goes back to a spoken-Romance \textbf{pettia}, a word the dictionaries star because nobody wrote it down. It is one of the small group of everyday words the Romans seem to have taken from the Gaulish spoken around them rather than brought with them, though that origin is offered with a hedge rather than asserted.

Now the part worth slowing down for. English \textbf{begin} comes from a Germanic verb with no piece in it anywhere. Two languages, no contact on this word, and both of them reached for the same image: starting is breaking into something whole.

English did keep \emph{pettia} by another road. A \textbf{piece} is the same word, arriving through French. So \emph{empezar} and \emph{piece} are relatives, and \emph{empezar} and \emph{begin} are strangers who happen to think alike.

One caution: the Academy marks the \emph{pettia} step as reconstructed. The line from \emph{pieza} to \emph{empezar} is firm; the line behind \emph{pieza} is a proposal.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the action: \emph{empezar}. And you can see a piece inside it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{empezar}
  \item \emph{empezar el libro}
  \item \emph{soñar}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which noun is hiding inside \emph{empezar}? (\emph{Pieza} — a piece.) And is English \emph{begin} related? (No — the same idea, built separately.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[acabar]{acabar — bringing a thing to its head}

\label{lesson:ES-C382-acabar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to dream}, then \emph{to begin}. (\emph{Soñar}; \emph{empezar}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item empezar — the opposite end of the same job.
  \item el libro — something you finish.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-ca-BAR}, three beats with the weight on the last. The \emph{c} before \emph{a} is a hard \emph{k}, and the \emph{b} between vowels is soft, closer to a \emph{v} made with both lips. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{acabar} — \textquotedblleft{}to finish.\textquotedblright{}

Inside it is \textbf{cabo}, which in Spanish means an end — and also a headland, the bit of land that runs out into the sea. Both senses come from Latin \textbf{caput}, a head. To \emph{acabar} something is to bring it to its head, its far end.

That metaphor is not unusual. What is unusual is that English built it twice, independently, and you use one of them constantly.

\textbf{Achieve} came into English from Old French \emph{achever}, and \emph{achever} is \emph{à chef} — \emph{chef} being the French descendant of the same \emph{caput}. To achieve is to come to a head. \emph{Acabar} and \emph{achieve} are not borrowings of one another. They are the same sentence written by two neighbours who each had the word for head and the same idea about what finishing is.

The family is large once you can see it. A \textbf{chief} is a head person. A \textbf{chef} is the head of a kitchen. \textbf{Capital} is head-money, a \textbf{captain} is a head-officer, and to \textbf{decapitate} is to remove one.

And Spanish kept the plain noun too: \textbf{la cabeza}, the head, which you already have. \emph{Cabo} and \emph{cabeza} are two children of \emph{caput} that grew up in different rooms.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the action: \emph{acabar}. And you can hear \emph{caput} in \emph{achieve}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{acabar}
  \item \emph{empezar y acabar}
  \item \emph{acabar el libro}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{caput} mean? (A head.) And what does \emph{achieve} take apart into? (The French \emph{à chef} — to a head.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pagar]{pagar — paying is making peace}

\label{lesson:ES-C382-pagar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to begin}, then \emph{to finish}. (\emph{Empezar}; \emph{acabar}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el dinero — what you pay with.
  \item el mercado — where.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pa-GAR}, two beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{g} before \emph{a} is hard, and between vowels it softens almost to nothing. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{pagar} — \textquotedblleft{}to pay.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{pacare} meant to pacify, to bring to peace. It was built on \textbf{pax}, peace, which you can still see in the \emph{pa-} at the front.

The road from peace to money is short once you stand where a Roman stood. If you owed somebody, there was a quarrel between you. To settle the debt was to settle the quarrel — to \emph{pacify} the creditor, so that no claim remained. Payment was the end of a dispute before it was a transaction.

English took the same verb by the same road, through French \emph{payer}, and so \textbf{pay} is \emph{pagar}'s sibling rather than its translation. Once you have that, the family opens up: \textbf{peace} itself, a \textbf{pact} (an agreement that ends an argument), to \textbf{appease}, and \textbf{pacific} — an ocean named for looking calm.

Now the trap. \textbf{Pagan} looks like it belongs here and does not. It comes from Latin \emph{paganus}, a country-dweller, from \emph{pagus}, a rural district. The two words share their first three letters and nothing else. A pagan is a villager, not a payer.

Spanish keeps the plain noun as well: \textbf{la paz}, peace — \emph{pax} with its ending worn off.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name the action: \emph{pagar}. And you know why paying and peace are one word.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pagar}
  \item \emph{pagar el pan}
  \item \emph{pagar en el mercado}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{pacare} mean? (To pacify, to bring to peace.) Is \emph{pagan} in this family? (No — that is \emph{pagus}, a village.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[quedar]{quedar — coming to rest}

\label{lesson:ES-C382-quedar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{to finish}, then \emph{to pay}. (\emph{Acabar}; \emph{pagar}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la casa — where you might stay.
  \item abajo — a place you might stay.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{que-DAR}, two beats with the weight on the second. \emph{Qu-} before \emph{e} is a plain \emph{k}; the \emph{u} is silent, doing nothing but keeping the \emph{c} hard. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{quedar} — \textquotedblleft{}to stay, to remain.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{quies} was rest or stillness, and \textbf{quietare} was to make something still. Spanish turned that into \emph{quedar}: to stay is to come to rest in a place rather than to move through it.

English helped itself to this root three separate times, and the three do not look like relatives.

\textbf{Quiet} is the closest — the adjective straight off \emph{quietus}, still.

\textbf{Quit} is the surprise. To quit was to release somebody from an obligation, to leave them in peace, and only later to leave a place or a job. A \textbf{requiem} is the same word again, asking rest for the dead.

And \textbf{coy} is the one nobody guesses. It came through French \emph{coi}, which meant still and quiet, from \emph{quietus}. Somebody described as coy was originally motionless and reserved. The modern flirtatious sense is a later drift, and the word has quietly kept its old meaning underneath.

Spanish also kept the adjective \textbf{quieto}, still, alongside the verb — the two sitting next to each other, one describing the state and one the act of arriving at it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name four more everyday actions: \emph{empezar}, \emph{acabar}, \emph{pagar}, \emph{quedar}. Say which one you did today.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{quedar}
  \item \emph{quedar en casa}
  \item \emph{empezar, acabar, pagar, quedar}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{quies} mean? (Rest, stillness.) And what did \emph{coy} mean before it meant teasing? (Still and reserved.)
\end{tcolorbox}
